source: Every curve on this page is drawn by evaluating the model itself, not by redrawing it — so it cannot come to describe something the app no longer does.

shape.title: How the notes are chosen
shape.intro: A melody here is not a random walk. Each note is drawn against a curve centred on the note before it, and the two shapes differ in one thing only: whether the rhythm gets a say in how wide that curve is.

order.title: The order things happen in
order.body: The rhythm is decided before any pitch is. That ordering is what makes the paced shape possible at all: by the time a note needs a pitch, it is already known how long there is before it.
order.step1: The bars are built one beat at a time, from the subdivisions the level allows. No pitches yet.
order.step2: The first note is drawn — preferring a member of the tonic triad, so the key has somewhere to be reckoned from.
order.step3: Every note after it is drawn in turn, left to right, each one against the note before it.

first.title: The note you are given
first.body: Its pitch is shown greyed on the staff before you write anything. Only its pitch — how long it lasts is a thing to hear, so it is not in the hint, and you type it yourself like every other note.

next.title: Every note after that
next.body: The notes available are the scale steps the level's range covers, and each one is given a weight. One is then drawn at random in proportion to those weights — so nothing is ever chosen by a rule that says yes or no, only by one that says more likely or less.
next.pools: Notes from outside the key are held back first: about one note in six is drawn from the chromatic notes and the rest from the scale's own, which is what keeps an altered note an event rather than a habit.

curves.figureLabel: Curves showing how likely each interval is, one for each length of gap. All three peak next to the last note; the longer the gap, the flatter the curve.
curves.caption: The curve is the same shape at every gap — only its width changes. The dots are the notes that actually exist to be chosen, at the shortest gap; the one in the middle sits below its own curve because a repeat is damped on purpose.

paced.title: Paced: the gap sets the width
paced.body: The weight falls away from the last note the further you go, and how fast it falls is the only thing the rhythm changes. After a sixteenth the curve is narrow, so steps and thirds take almost all of it. After a half note the same curve is smeared out, and an octave is an ordinary move.
paced.width: The width grows with the gap and then stops. The cap is deliberate: without it a long note would eventually make every interval equally likely, which is the aimless line this exists to avoid.
paced.concrete: What that comes to for the moves you can name, as a share of the likeliest move at that gap:

width.figureLabel: A rising curve showing the width of the interval curve against the length of the gap, flattening at its cap.
width.caption: How wide the curve is, in semitones, against how long there is before the note: about {{narrow}} after a sixteenth and {{wide}} after a whole note. Past {{beats}} beats it stops growing.

steady.title: Steady: one table, every note
steady.body: The other shape uses a fixed table of weights and never consults the rhythm. Steps are still far likelier than leaps, but a wide interval can land on a quick note — which is harder to hear, and is the point of the option rather than a flaw in it.
steady.figureLabel: A bar chart of the fixed weights by interval: a staircase that steps down in blocks rather than falling away smoothly.
steady.caption: A staircase rather than a curve: within a block every interval is equally likely, and the block is the same whatever the rhythm.

compare.caption: Read across a row to see the same interval get likelier as there is more time for it. The unison is the exception: it is damped at every gap.

rules.title: What is guaranteed
rules.body: Whatever the shape and whatever the gap, four things always hold:
rules.range: The range you set is the only hard boundary. Nothing outside it is ever drawn, and everything inside it can be.
rules.nothing: No interval inside the range is ever impossible. The curve gets very small, never zero, so even a wide leap after a sixteenth will happen eventually.
rules.unison: Repeating a note is always possible and always damped — the rhythm tells two notes on one pitch apart, but a line that sits still is not asking you anything.
rules.rhythm: The shape changes the pitches and never the rhythm. The same seed gives the same bars under either setting.

figures.title: How a figure is read
figures.intro: A figure is not the name of a chord. It is a set of intervals measured up from the bass, and read against the key signature.

reading.title: Count up from the bass
reading.body: A 6 means the note a sixth above the bass. Not a particular note — the sixth over D is B, the sixth over E is C, and the same figure is a different note under every bass note it stands beneath.
reading.key: Which B or which C is the key signature's business. In C major the sixth over D is B natural; in F major, where the signature flattens it, the same 6 over the same D is B flat. The figure never says; the signature already did.

omission.title: What is left out
omission.body: A figure writes only what is not taken for granted, and the shorthand is most of what there is to learn. It is why an unfigured bass note is not a bass note with no chord on it.
omission.plain: No figure at all means the common chord — a third and a fifth over the bass.
omission.sixth: 6 means a sixth and a third. The third goes without saying, so writing 6/3 says something that did not need saying.
omission.seventh: 7 means a seventh, a fifth and a third: everything under the seventh is assumed.
omission.second: 2 means a sixth, a fourth and a second. 4/2 is the same figure written a little longer, and both are current.
omission.accidental: A line carrying an accidental is always written, whatever the shorthand would drop — the accidental is exactly the thing not taken for granted.

table.title: Every figure this exercise uses
table.body: Written on the left, what it stands for in the middle, and what it comes to over one bass note on the right. The key belongs to the row: a flattened third says nothing in a key that gives a natural one.

accidentals.title: Sharps, flats and naturals
accidentals.body: An accidental before a number moves that note a semitone from what the key gives it. In G major the fifth over E flat is B natural, so ♭5 asks for B flat — not for B double flat, which reading the sign as absolute would give.
accidentals.bare: An accidental standing alone, with no number beside it, belongs to the third. That is the commonest figure in the repertoire after 6: it is how the raised third of a dominant in a minor key is written.

figures.source: The rules here follow the article on Thoroughbass in A Dictionary of Music and Musicians, and the table is computed from the same model the exercise grades against.
